corpus_definition: to provide something that people need

forms.definition: an amount of something that is ready for people to use
forms.example: The town has a good supply of clean water.
forms.note: Often plural: supplies = food, tools and other things people need, as in 'office supplies'.

syn.note: An amount of goods kept ready to use or sell; common in shops.
Related: an amount of something kept for later use.
Related: an amount kept for a time when you need it, like oil or water reserves.

ant.note: A shortage means there is not enough of something.
In business, supply is what is offered and demand is what people want to buy.

forms.definition: to give people things that they need or want
forms.example: This farm supplies milk to shops in Tashkent.
forms.note: Patterns: supply something to someone; supply someone with something.

syn.note: Almost the same; provide is very common and a little more general.
Easy everyday word; supply is used more for goods and services, often regularly.
Formal: furnish someone with information or goods.
Related: to take goods to a place; supply is about giving what is needed.

forms.note: There is no common adjective made from supply. Don't confuse with supple (bending easily), which is a different word.
There is no adverb made from supply.

people.definition: a person or company that sells goods to businesses
people.example: Our supplier sends new parts to the factory every week.

context.text: A local farm supplies fresh vegetables to our school. When the supply of tomatoes runs low, the cook calls the supplier and asks for more.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same meaning merged (lowest CEFR B1). Supplier (y to i + -er) kept in People & things; supple is not family.

corpus_definition: feeling shocked because something was unexpected
usage_note: be surprised at + noun / how, what clause: 'I was surprised at the price.' 'We were surprised at how big it was.' Surprised by is also common and means the same.

relations.note: Same meaning; by is a little more common in modern English.
Stronger: very surprised, often in a good way.
Very surprised; a little more formal.
Related: surprised in a bad or upsetting way.

context.text: My grandmother was surprised at how well I can cook plov now. I was surprised at her reaction too, because she usually says nothing.

reviewer_note: kind_hint was phrasal; corrected to phrase (adjective + preposition, not verb + particle).

corpus_definition: feeling that something might be wrong or dishonest

forms.definition: a feeling that someone has done something wrong
forms.example: I have a suspicion that he is not telling the truth.

syn.note: A feeling that you cannot trust someone; a bit more general.
Very close to distrust; a little more formal.
Related: a feeling that something may not be true.

ant.note: Trust is the belief that someone is honest and good.

forms.definition: to think that someone may have done something wrong
forms.example: The teacher suspected that Aziz had copied his homework.
forms.note: Also a noun with stress on the first syllable: a suspect = a person the police think did a crime.

syn.note: Related: to feel you cannot trust someone; suspect is about thinking they did something wrong.
Related: close to distrust, a little more formal.

ant.note: To trust someone is to believe they are honest.

forms.definition: feeling that someone may be dishonest or that something is wrong
forms.example: My mother was suspicious of the man selling cheap phones.
forms.note: Also means 'making you feel that something is wrong': a suspicious bag at the station. Pattern: suspicious of someone.

syn.note: Not trusting someone; a little more formal.
Careful because you think there may be a danger or problem.
Related: not sure that something is true or good.

ant.note: A trusting person believes that others are honest.

forms.definition: in a way that shows you think something is wrong
forms.example: The guard looked at us suspiciously when we came in.
forms.note: Also: in a way that makes people think something is wrong: 'He was acting suspiciously.'

syn.note: Close in meaning but much less common.
Related: in a way that shows you are not sure.

context.text: The shop owner became suspicious when a customer paid with a very old banknote. He had a suspicion it was fake, so he looked at it suspiciously under the light.

reviewer_note: suspect (noun, a person) not added to People & things because suspect already appears as the verb form; mentioned in its note. No -ous affix claimed (suspici- is not a word).

corpus_definition: To use very bad or rude language when you are angry.

forms.definition: the use of rude or offensive words
forms.example: There is too much swearing in that film for children.

syn.note: Easy phrase with the same meaning.
Very close; a little old-fashioned in British English.

forms.definition: to use rude or offensive words, often when you are angry
forms.example: He swore loudly when he dropped the hot pan.
forms.note: Irregular: swear, swore, sworn. Pattern: swear at someone.

syn.note: Same meaning; a little more formal or old-fashioned.
Informal American English.

forms.definition: made after a very serious, formal promise to tell the truth
forms.example: The witness gave a sworn statement to the court.
forms.note: Belongs to swear = make a serious promise, not using rude words.
There is no adverb made from swear.

context.text: My little brother heard a word on the bus and asked me what it meant. I told him it was swearing and that people who swear in front of children are rude.

reviewer_note: swear has two corpus meanings; this map is rude language, the promise row has its own map. Compound swear word left out.

corpus_definition: to make a very serious promise; to use very bad language

forms.definition: the use of rude or offensive words
forms.example: The coach does not allow swearing during practice.
forms.note: Belongs to swear = use rude words, not making a promise. For a serious promise English uses oath or vow.

forms.definition: to promise very seriously that something is true or that you will do it
forms.example: I swear I didn't take your phone.
forms.note: Irregular: swear, swore, sworn. Patterns: swear (that) + clause; swear to do something.

syn.note: Easy everyday word; swear is stronger and more serious.
A very serious promise, often formal or in stories.
Formal promise, often in public or in politics.
Related: to promise that something will happen or be true.

forms.definition: made after a serious, formal promise to tell the truth
forms.example: She gave a sworn statement to the police.
forms.note: Also in 'sworn enemies' = people who have decided to be enemies for ever.

syn.note: Related: a sworn statement is an official one, made under a formal promise.

forms.note: There is no adverb made from swear.

context.text: Dilnoza swore she would call her parents every Sunday while she studied abroad. In court, the witness was sworn in and gave a sworn statement.

reviewer_note: CORPUS: this row's definition mixes both meanings; its example is the promise meaning, so the map follows promise. Rude-language meaning has its own map (row 6a42816a...).

forms.definition: the quality of being very fast
forms.example: Everyone was surprised by the swiftness of his recovery.

syn.note: Everyday word for how fast something is.
Same meaning; a little more common in speech.
Formal, mostly in writing.

ant.note: The quality of not moving or happening fast.

forms.note: There is no verb made from swift.

forms.definition: moving or happening very quickly
forms.example: The police took swift action after the accident.
forms.note: A little more formal or literary than fast or quick; common in news: a swift response.

syn.note: Easy everyday word with the same meaning.
Easy everyday word; often about actions that take little time.
Same meaning; a little formal, common in writing.
Often in wishes: a speedy recovery.

forms.definition: very quickly
forms.example: The boat moved swiftly down the river.

syn.note: Easy everyday word with the same meaning.
Same meaning; a little formal.
Fast is also an adverb: run fast.

context.text: The doctors in Samarkand acted swiftly when my uncle fell ill. Thanks to their swift help, he was home in a week.

reviewer_note: swift is also a bird (noun); left out as a separate word, not part of the 'fast' family for learners.

corpus_definition: To change from one thing or action to another.

forms.definition: a change from one thing or way of doing something to another
forms.example: The switch to online lessons was difficult for many teachers.
forms.note: The same noun also means the small button that turns a light or machine on or off.

syn.note: Easy general word with the same meaning.
A change of direction, opinion or method; often gradual.
Related: an exchange of one thing for another.

forms.definition: to change from one thing, plan or activity to another
forms.example: I switched from coffee to green tea last year.
forms.note: Patterns: switch from A to B; switch to something. Phrasal verbs switch on / switch off are about lights and machines.

syn.note: Easy general word with the same meaning.
Often a slower or smaller change.
Related: to give one thing and get another in its place; informal.
Related: to put a new thing in the place of an old one.

forms.note: There is no common adjective made from switch in this meaning.
There is no adverb made from switch.

context.text: Many students in Tashkent switched to online classes last winter. The switch was hard at first, but now they like studying from home.

reviewer_note: Noun switch = change shown as conversion; device meaning only noted. Compound switchboard left out.

corpus_definition: a long piece of serious music for a full orchestra

forms.definition: a long piece of classical music for a large orchestra
forms.example: We listened to a Mozart symphony at the concert hall.
forms.note: Also used in names of orchestras: the London Symphony Orchestra.

syn.note: Related: a long piece for an orchestra and one main player, like a pianist.
Related: any piece of music someone has written.

forms.note: There is no verb made from symphony.

forms.definition: connected with music written for a large orchestra
forms.example: The film has beautiful symphonic music.

syn.note: Played by or written for an orchestra; a little more general.

forms.note: There is no common adverb made from symphony.

context.text: The orchestra in Tashkent played a symphony by Beethoven on Friday. My sister loves symphonic music, so she bought tickets for the whole family.

reviewer_note: No -ic affix claimed: symphonic replaces the -y, and symphon- is not a word. Symphony orchestra is a compound, left out.

corpus_definition: to return something to a store for a refund
particle_note: Separable: 'take back the shoes' or 'take the shoes back'; with a pronoun only 'take them back'. Often: take something back to the shop.

relations.note: Same meaning; a little more formal: return an item to the shop.
Same idea, said from the shop's point of view: 'bring it back with the receipt'.
Related: you take something back and get a different one, not your money.
You keep the thing you bought and do not return it.

context.text: The jacket I bought at the market was too small, so I took it back the next day. The seller said I could take back any item within a week.

reviewer_note: Other meanings of take back (say you were wrong about something you said; remind of the past) are not this map.

corpus_definition: Naturally good at doing a specific activity.
usage_note: be talented at + noun / -ing: 'She is talented at drawing.' Talented in is also used, and talented often comes before a noun: a talented singer.

relations.note: Easy everyday phrase; talented at stresses natural ability.
Very close; often about children with special ability.
Related: good because of training and practice, not only natural ability.
Not able to do something well.

context.text: My cousin Jasur is very talented at playing the dutar. His teacher says he is the most talented at music in the whole school.

reviewer_note: Fixed adjective + preposition pattern; no forms.

corpus_definition: Money that you pay to the government.

forms.definition: money that people and companies must pay to the government
forms.example: We pay tax on everything we buy in the shop.

syn.note: Money paid to the government on goods, especially goods brought into a country.
Formal word for an official charge.
Related: money paid on goods coming into or going out of a country.
Related: money you pay for a service, not to the government in general.

forms.definition: the system of making people pay money to the government
forms.example: High taxation makes life hard for small businesses.

forms.definition: to make people pay money to the government on something
forms.example: The government taxes cigarettes very heavily.

syn.note: Related: formal, used with the tax as object: levy a tax on fuel.
Related: to ask for money for something.

forms.definition: that you must pay money to the government on
forms.example: Most of his income is taxable.

ant.note: If something is tax-free, you do not pay money to the government on it.

forms.definition: needing a lot of effort, so it makes you tired
forms.example: Teaching forty children every day is a taxing job.
forms.note: Belongs to tax = put a heavy load on someone, not paying money to the government.
There is no adverb made from tax.

context.text: In Uzbekistan, most workers pay income tax every month. The government also taxes some goods, like cars brought in from abroad, and any taxable income must be reported.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same meaning merged. taxing (tiring) shown as other_meaning false friend. Compounds taxpayer, taxman, tax-free (only as antonym) not shown as forms.
